title: Impulse
lead: Newton’s second law, written with the change in momentum, gives the product of a force and the time it acts a name of its own, the impulse. You see what it means for a ball bouncing off a rigid wall, for a passenger brought to rest by a dashboard or an airbag, and for a force that is never constant.
objectives: Describe effects of impulses in everyday life.
Determine the average effective force using graphical representation.
Calculate average force and impulse given mass, velocity, and time.
summary_html:
• Impulse, or change in momentum, equals the average net external force multiplied by the time this force acts: $\kdp = \kFnet\kdt.$
  • Forces are usually not constant over a period of time.

exercises.prompt: Explain in terms of impulse how padding reduces forces in a collision. State this in terms of a real example, such as the advantages of a carpeted vs. tile floor for a day care center.

answer.solution: Padding works by stretching the collision out in time. Whatever you land on, your momentum must drop to zero, and your mass and speed fix the change in momentum; it is the same on carpet as on tile. The padding changes how long the stop takes. The change in momentum equals the average net external force multiplied by the time it acts, so a stop that lasts ten times as long needs only a tenth of the force. In a day care center, a carpeted floor lets a child’s head or wrist come to rest over a few hundredths of a second instead of a few thousandths. The force on the bone is smaller in the same proportion, often the difference between a bruise and a fracture.

exercises.prompt: While jumping on a trampoline, sometimes you land on your back and other times on your feet. In which case can you reach a greater height and why?

answer.solution: You can reach a greater height when you land on your feet. In both landings the trampoline must reverse your momentum, and the impulse it gives you is its force multiplied by the time it acts. Landing on your feet, you meet the bed over a small area, the bed stretches a long way, and your legs stand between you and it. You can straighten them as the bed pushes back and add your own work to what the bed returns, so the upward impulse exceeds the one that stopped you. Landing on your back spreads the contact over a large area, the bed stretches much less, and nothing you do adds to the push. More of the energy goes into deforming you and the bed than into throwing you back up. The landing on your back is gentler, and the lost height is the price.

exercises.prompt: Tennis racquets have “sweet spots.” If the ball hits a sweet spot then the player's arm is not jarred as much as it would be otherwise. Explain why this is the case.

answer.solution: A racquet held in the hand can move back with the ball and can also turn about the place your hand holds it. A ball that strikes away from the sweet spot does both: it pushes the head back and twists the handle, and your arm must supply whatever force keeps the handle in place. That force acts over the few thousandths of a second the ball stays on the strings, and it is what jars you. At the sweet spot, the turning and the pushing back cancel at the handle. The racquet moves without twisting in your hand, and your arm supplies only the small impulse that goes with the recoil of the whole racquet. The ball’s change in momentum is much the same wherever it strikes; what changes is how much of the force behind it reaches your arm.

exercises.prompt: A 1.0-kg ball of putty is released from rest and falls vertically 1.5 m until it strikes a hard floor, where it comes to rest in a 0.045-s time interval. What is the magnitude and direction of the average force exerted on the ball by the floor during the collision?

answer.hint: Find the speed the putty has reached after falling 1.5 m, turn that into a momentum, and divide by the time the floor takes to remove it.

exercises.prompt: A 75-g ball is dropped from rest from a height of 2.2 m. It bounces off the floor and rebounds to a maximum height of 1.7 m. If the ball is in contact with the floor for 0.024 s, what is the magnitude and direction of the average force exerted on the ball by the floor during the collision?

answer.solution: The floor exerts an average force of about 39 N, directed upward. Take up as positive. Falling from rest through 2.2 m, the ball reaches the floor with speed $\sqrt{2\kg\kh} = \sqrt{2(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)(2.2\ \text{m})} = 6.57\ \text{m/s}$, so $\kvi = -6.57\ \text{m/s}$. Rising to 1.7 m means it left the floor at $\sqrt{2(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)(1.7\ \text{m})} = 5.77\ \text{m/s}$, so $\kvf = +5.77\ \text{m/s}$. The change in momentum is $\kdp = \km(\kvf - \kvi) = (0.075\ \text{kg})(12.34\ \text{m/s}) = 0.926\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$, upward. The average net force is $\kFnet = \kdp/\kdt = (0.926\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s})/(0.024\ \text{s}) = 38.6\ \text{N}$. The net force is the floor's push minus the ball's weight, $\km\kg = (0.075\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2) = 0.74\ \text{N}$, so the floor's force is $38.6\ \text{N} + 0.74\ \text{N} = 39\ \text{N}$ upward.

exercises.prompt: A 2.4-kg ceramic bowl falls to the floor. During the 0.018-s impact, the bowl experiences an average force of 750 N from the floor. The bowl is at rest after the impact. From what initial height did the bowl fall?

answer.hint: The impulse the floor gives the bowl is the momentum the bowl arrived with, so work from the force and the time back to a speed, and from the speed back to a height.

exercises.prompt: Whether or not an object (such as a plate, glass, or bone) breaks upon impact depends on the average force exerted on that object by the surface. When a 1.2-kg glass figure hits the floor, it will break if it experiences an average force of 330 N. When it hits a tile floor, the glass comes to a stop in 0.015 s. From what minimum height must the glass fall to experience sufficient force to break? How would your answer change if the figure were falling to a padded or carpeted surface? Explain.

answer.solution: The glass must fall from at least about 0.87 m, and onto a padded or carpeted surface it would have to fall from higher still. A force of 330 N acting for 0.015 s changes the momentum of the glass by $\kdp = \kFnet\kdt = (330\ \text{N})(0.015\ \text{s}) = 4.95\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$; the 12 N weight of the glass is small beside 330 N and is neglected. The glass ends at rest, so this is the momentum it has on arrival, and its arrival speed is $\kv = \kdp/\km = (4.95\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s})/(1.2\ \text{kg}) = 4.13\ \text{m/s}$. A body falling from rest reaches this speed after a fall of $\kh = \kv^2/2\kg = (4.13\ \text{m/s})^2/2(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2) = 0.87\ \text{m}$. A lower fall gives a smaller arrival speed, a smaller change in momentum over the same 0.015 s, and so a force below 330 N. A padded or carpeted surface stops the glass over a longer time. The same change in momentum spread over a longer $\kdt$ means a smaller force, so the glass must arrive faster, from a greater height, before the force reaches 330 N.

exercises.prompt:
A 2.5-kg block slides across a frictionless table toward a horizontal spring. As the block bounces off the spring, a probe measures the velocity of the block (initially negative, moving away from the probe) over time as follows:
Velocity (m/s)Time (s)
−12.00
−10.00.10
−6.00.20
00.30
6.00.40
10.00.50
12.00.60
What is the average force exerted on the block by the spring over the entire 0.60-s time interval of the collision?

answer.hint: Only the first and the last rows of the table matter: they give the velocity before and after, and the whole of the change happens in 0.60 s.
answer.solution: (c) (based on calculation of $F = \frac{m\Delta v}{\Delta t}$)

exercises.prompt: During an automobile crash test, the average force exerted by a solid wall on a 2500-kg car that hits the wall is measured to be 740,000 N over a 0.22-s time interval. What was the initial speed of the car prior to the collision, assuming the car is at rest at the end of the time interval?

answer.solution: The car was traveling at about 65 m/s. The wall brings the car to rest, so the impulse it delivers equals the whole of the car's initial momentum. The magnitude of that impulse is $\kFnet\kdt = (740{,}000\ \text{N})(0.22\ \text{s}) = 1.63 \times 10^{5}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$. The force acts against the motion, so $\kdp = \km(0 - \kvi) = -1.63 \times 10^{5}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$, which gives $\kvi = (1.63 \times 10^{5}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s})/(2500\ \text{kg}) = 65\ \text{m/s}$, toward the wall.

exercises.prompt: A test car is driving toward a solid crash-test barrier with a speed of 45 mi/h. Two seconds prior to impact, the car begins to brake, but it is still moving when it hits the wall. After the collision with the wall, the car crumples somewhat and comes to a complete stop. In order to estimate the average force exerted by the wall on the car, what information would you need to collect?

options: The (negative) acceleration of the car before it hits the wall and the distance the car travels while braking.
The (negative) acceleration of the car before it hits the wall and the velocity of the car just before impact.
The velocity of the car just before impact and the duration of the collision with the wall.
The duration of the collision with the wall and the distance the car travels while braking.
answer.hint: The force during the collision follows from the change in momentum and the time the collision takes, and nothing that happens during the braking enters it.

exercises.prompt: Design an experiment to verify the relationship between the average force exerted on an object and the change in momentum of that object. As part of your explanation, list the equipment you would use and describe your experimental setup. What would you measure and how? How exactly would you verify the relationship? Explain.

answer.solution: A cart running into a sprung force sensor verifies the relationship. The equipment is a cart of known mass on a level, low-friction track, a force sensor mounted on the front of the cart with a spring bumper on it, a rigid stop at the end of the track, a motion sensor at the far end watching the cart, and a balance for weighing the cart with the sensor on it. The cart is pushed toward the stop, and the force sensor records force against time while the motion sensor records velocity against time, right through the collision. The change in momentum is the mass of the cart multiplied by the difference between the steady velocities just before and just after the bounce, $\kdp = \km(\kvf - \kvi)$. The impulse is the area under the force-against-time curve, which equals $\kFnet\kdt$ for the average force over the contact time. Repeating the run at several speeds and with bumpers of different stiffness gives a range of values, and a graph of impulse against change in momentum verifies the relationship if its points lie on a straight line through the origin with slope one. The largest uncertainties come from friction and a track that is not quite level, which add external forces, and from the edges of the force pulse; levelling the track and keeping the speeds high relative to friction reduces them.

exercises.prompt: A 22-g puck hits the wall of an air hockey table perpendicular to the wall with an initial speed of 14 m/s. The puck is in contact with the wall for 0.0055 s, and it rebounds from the wall with a speed of 14 m/s in the opposite direction. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the puck?

answer.hint: The puck arrives going one way and leaves going the other, so the change in its momentum is twice $m\kv$, not once.

exercises.prompt: A 22-g puck hits the wall of an air hockey table perpendicular to the wall with an initial speed of 7 m/s. The puck is in contact with the wall for 0.011 s, and the wall exerts an average force of 28 N on the puck during that time. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the change in momentum of the puck.

answer.solution: The change in momentum is 0.31 kg·m/s, directed away from the wall. The change in momentum equals the impulse, $\kdp = \kFnet\kdt = (28\ \text{N})(0.011\ \text{s}) = 0.308\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$, and it points the way the force does, out from the wall and opposite to the puck's original motion. The puck arrives with momentum $\km\kv = (0.022\ \text{kg})(7\ \text{m/s}) = 0.154\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ toward the wall. The change is twice this, so the wall first removes all of the puck's momentum and then gives it as much again in the opposite direction: the puck rebounds at 7 m/s.

exercises.prompt: The graph shown represents the force exerted on a particle during a collision. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the particle as a result of the collision?

answer.solution: The change in momentum is $3.6\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$. The change in momentum equals the impulse, which is the area under the graph of force against time. The force rises linearly from zero at $\kt = 0$ to 15 N at 0.080 s, holds at 15 N until 0.24 s, and falls linearly to zero at 0.32 s, so the area is a trapezoid. Its bottom side spans 0.32 s and its top side spans $0.24\ \text{s} - 0.080\ \text{s} = 0.16\ \text{s}$, so the area is $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.32\ \text{s} + 0.16\ \text{s})(15\ \text{N}) = 3.6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$. Cutting the shape into two triangles and a rectangle gives the same result: $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.080\ \text{s})(15\ \text{N}) + (0.16\ \text{s})(15\ \text{N}) + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.080\ \text{s})(15\ \text{N}) = 0.60 + 2.4 + 0.60 = 3.6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$, and $1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

exercises.prompt: A bullet is accelerated down the barrel of a gun by hot gases produced in the combustion of gun powder. What is the average force exerted on a 0.0300-kg bullet to accelerate it to a speed of 600.0 m/s in a time of 2.00 ms (milliseconds)?

answer.hint: The bullet starts at rest, so the change in momentum is the whole of $m\kv$. Turn the milliseconds into seconds before you divide.

exercises.prompt: A person slaps her leg with her hand, bringing her hand to rest in 2.50 milliseconds from an initial speed of 4.00 m/s. (a) What is the average force exerted on the leg, taking the effective mass of the hand and forearm to be 1.50 kg? (b) Would the force be any different if the woman clapped her hands together at the same speed and brought them to rest in the same time? Explain why or why not.

answer.hint: Take the change in momentum of the hand and forearm and divide it by the 2.50 ms the stop takes.
answer.solution: (a) $2.40\times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$ toward the leg. (b) The force on each hand would have the same magnitude as that found in part (a) (but in opposite directions by Newton’s third law) because the change in momentum and the time interval are the same.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a child drives a bumper car head on into the side rail, which exerts a force of 4000 N on the car for 0.200 s. (a) What impulse is imparted by this force? (b) Find the final velocity of the bumper car if its initial velocity was 2.80 m/s and the car plus driver have a mass of 200 kg. You may neglect friction between the car and floor.

parts.hint: The impulse is the force multiplied by the time it acts, and nothing else enters part (a).
Add the impulse to the initial momentum, keeping the signs, and divide by the mass.

answer.solution: (a) 800 kg⋅m/s away from the wall. (b) 1.20 m/s away from the wall.

exercises.prompt: A 75.0-kg person is riding in a car moving at 20.0 m/s when the car runs into a bridge abutment. (a) Calculate the average force on the person if he is stopped by a padded dashboard that compresses an average of 1.00 cm. (b) Calculate the average force on the person if he is stopped by an air bag that compresses an average of 15.0 cm.

parts.hint: The distance tells you the time: over the stop the average speed is half the initial speed, so 1.00 cm at 10.0 m/s takes a thousandth of a second.
The same change in momentum, but the air bag gives it fifteen times as long to happen.

answer.solution: (a) $1.50\times 10^{6}\ \text{N}$ away from the dashboard. (b) $1.00\times 10^{5}\ \text{N}$ away from the dashboard.

exercises.prompt: A cruise ship with a mass of $1.00\times 10^{7}\ \text{kg}$ strikes a pier at a speed of 0.750 m/s. It comes to rest 6.00 m later, damaging the ship, the pier, and the tugboat captain’s finances. Calculate the average force exerted on the pier using the concept of impulse. (Hint: First calculate the time it took to bring the ship to rest.)

answer.hint: The ship slows steadily, so its average speed over the 6.00 m is half of 0.750 m/s, and that is what gives you the time.
answer.solution: $4.69\times 10^{5}\ \text{N}$ in the boat’s original direction of motion

exercises.prompt: Water from a fire hose is directed horizontally against a wall at a rate of 50.0 kg/s and a speed of 42.0 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the force exerted on the wall, assuming the water’s horizontal momentum is reduced to zero.

answer.hint: A rate in kilograms a second is a mass divided by a time already, so the momentum removed each second is that rate multiplied by the speed.
answer.solution: $2.10\times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$ away from the wall

exercises.prompt: Starting with the definitions of momentum and kinetic energy, derive an equation for the kinetic energy of a particle expressed as a function of its momentum.

answer.solution: $$\begin{array}{l}\kp = m\kv \Rightarrow \kp^{2} = m^{2}\kv^{2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\kp^{2}}{m} = m\kv^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \dfrac{\kp^{2}}{2m} = \dfrac{1}{2}m\kv^{2} = \kKE \\ \kKE = \dfrac{\kp^{2}}{2m}\end{array}$$

exercises.prompt: When serving a tennis ball, a player hits the ball when its velocity is zero (at the highest point of a vertical toss). The racquet exerts a force of 540 N on the ball for 5.00 ms, giving it a final velocity of 45.0 m/s. Using these data, find the mass of the ball.

answer.hint: Work out the impulse first; the ball starts from rest, so that impulse is $m\kv$, and the mass is all that is left unknown.
